Roofing

Asphalt Shingle Roofing for Texas Homes

The right shingle for a hail corridor with 100-degree summers is a different conversation than the one they have in Oregon.

Schedule a Free Inspection 469-371-9599
  • Free inspectionsLicensed inspector, on your roof
  • Free estimatesWritten, itemised, no obligation
  • Fully insuredCover in place before we start
  • Licensed inspectorsAssessing, not selling
  • DFW and North TexasRoughly two hours from Dallas

Asphalt shingles cover the overwhelming majority of homes in North Texas, and for good reason: strong wind performance, sane cost, wide color range, and repairability. The differences that matter here are impact rating, weight, wind rating, and how the product handles sustained heat.

Color is not only an appearance decision in this climate. Darker roofs run hotter, and attic ventilation has to keep up either way. We will walk you through the options against your brick, your trim, and any HOA requirements.

When asphalt shingle roofing is worth looking into

You are choosing a replacement product

This is the decision that determines how the roof performs for the next two decades.

Your current roof is three-tab

Older three-tab roofs are common on North Texas homes built before the 2000s and generally underperform modern architectural products in wind.

You are weighing impact-resistant shingles

Worth a real conversation in this region, including the trade-offs nobody mentions.

Causes

What causes it

Heat degradation

Sustained high surface temperatures age the asphalt mat and soften sealant bonds.

Hail impact

Granule loss and mat bruising are the standard failure mode in this market.

Wind uplift

Wind rating and correct nailing pattern matter more than most homeowners are told.

Our inspection

How we look at it

  • Confirm existing shingle type, layer count, and condition
  • Assess deck and ventilation before recommending a product
  • Review color options against the home's brick, stone, and trim
  • Check any HOA or neighborhood requirements you are aware of

North Texas conditions

Sun exposure in North Texas means the south and west slopes almost always show wear first, so any product comparison should be judged on those slopes rather than on the shaded north side of the house.

Options

Materials and approaches

Architectural / dimensional

Laminated construction, dimensional shadow line, and higher wind ratings than three-tab. The default recommendation for most homes here.

Impact-resistant (Class 4)

Tested to resist impact better than standard shingles. Higher material cost, and some insurers treat them differently — ask your carrier, not us, about premium implications.

Three-tab

Flat appearance and lower cost. Occasionally right for outbuildings or budget-constrained rentals.

Designer profiles

Heavier laminated shingles that imitate slate or shake, for homes where the roof is a major part of the elevation.

Synthetic underlayment

Tear-resistant and far more stable underfoot than felt, and it holds up if weather arrives mid-job.

Ice-and-water membrane

Self-adhering protection in the valleys and around every penetration, where the water actually concentrates.

Not sure which of these you need?

That is what the free inspection is for. A licensed inspector will tell you what your roof actually requires.

In detail

What actually differs between products

Shingle marketing runs on names and colours. The specifications that change how a roof performs in North Texas are a shorter list: wind rating, impact rating, weight and laminate construction, and the fastening pattern the manufacturer requires.

Architectural shingles are laminated — two or more layers bonded together, giving them dimensional shadow lines, more weight, and meaningfully better wind performance than the three-tab products that cover many older homes here. That extra weight and the wider nailing zone are most of why they hold up better, not the appearance.

Impact rating is measured separately from wind. A Class 4 product has been tested against impact specifically, and in a hail corridor that is a distinct and relevant question from how it handles a gust.

The accessories decide more than the shingle does

A premium shingle installed over reused flashing, with no valley membrane and cracked boots left in place, will underperform a mid-range shingle installed properly. This is consistently true and consistently under-discussed, because accessories do not have brand recognition.

The list worth asking about on any estimate: synthetic underlayment across the deck, ice-and-water membrane in valleys and around penetrations, new drip edge, new step and counter flashing at walls and chimneys, new pipe boots on every vent, correct starter course at eaves and rakes, and a ventilation plan that accounts for intake as well as exhaust.

Those lines are where estimates genuinely differ, and they are also where a roof's real service life is decided.

Colour, heat, and the energy claim

Darker shingles run hotter at the surface. That is straightforwardly true. What is frequently oversold is the leap from that fact to a meaningful change in your electricity bill.

Attic insulation depth and functioning ventilation influence what you actually pay far more than shingle colour does. If someone is selling you a lighter roof primarily on energy savings and has not looked in your attic, they have skipped the part that matters. We would rather fix your intake ventilation and let you pick the colour you like.

Questions

Asphalt Shingle Roofing FAQs

Are impact-resistant shingles worth it in DFW?

They can be, particularly if you have been hit more than once. They cost more and they are not indestructible. Some insurance carriers treat them differently — that is a question for your carrier, and we will not make claims about your premium.

Does shingle color affect my energy bill?

Color affects roof surface temperature, but attic insulation and ventilation have far more influence on what you actually pay. We would rather fix your ventilation than sell you a color story.

How many layers can a roof have?

We tear off rather than layer over, so this mostly matters for what we find during removal. Multiple existing layers add weight, hide deck problems, and increase disposal cost.
